questions.q: Why does naively quoting a market maker's bid and ask around the last traded price fail?
options: Regulators prohibit using the last trade price as a reference
The last traded price is always identical to the midpoint, so there is no real difference
The last trade already happened, so it reflects where the market was, not where it is -- if the market has moved since, one side of the quote is already wrong and can be picked off
Salesforce does not allow quoting around the last trade price
questions.explain: The last trade is a snapshot of the past; in any liquid instrument the market continues moving after it, making it a stale and exploitable anchor.

questions.q: What does the microprice do differently from the plain midpoint?
options: It only considers the ask price, never the bid
It ignores order book size entirely and uses only the last trade
It weights each side of the quote by the OTHER side's size, pulling the estimate toward the side with less resting size
It is always exactly equal to the midpoint by definition
questions.explain: The microprice weights the bid by ask size and the ask by bid size -- a large resting bid pulls the estimate toward the ask, reflecting the buying pressure that size signals.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, why does the microprice sit much closer to the ask (100.0596) than the midpoint (100.0400)?
options: The large resting bid size (5,000 vs. 50 on the ask) signals real buying interest that pulls the fair-value estimate toward the ask
The microprice formula always favors the ask side regardless of sizes
The ask price itself was much higher in this example than the bid
A calculation error caused the discrepancy
questions.explain: A much larger bid size relative to ask size is exactly the imbalance the microprice is designed to react to, pulling the estimate toward the thinner (ask) side.

questions.q: What is the real risk of a market maker having a bad fair-value estimate, according to this lesson?
options: A bad fair-value estimate only affects the first few trades of the day
Fair value estimation only matters for options market making, not equities
Every downstream quoting decision (reservation price, inventory skew, adverse-selection defense) inherits the error, since they all build on top of the fair-value anchor
There is no real risk, since spread capture compensates for estimation error automatically
questions.explain: Every later lesson's logic is built on top of the fair-value estimate -- an error here propagates into every downstream decision, which is more dangerous than imperfect logic built on a correct estimate.

questions.q: Where does the line between "market making" and "short-horizon alpha generation" genuinely blur, per this lesson?
options: Only when a market maker stops quoting both sides of the market
Market making and alpha generation are completely unrelated disciplines with no overlap
When a market maker layers a short-horizon statistical model on top of the microprice to get a better fair-value estimate than competitors
The blur only happens in options markets, never in equities
questions.explain: A market maker with a genuinely better short-horizon fair-value model has a real edge beyond the spread alone -- this is exactly where the two disciplines overlap in practice.
